# Maths S11 D02: What privacy, bias and ethics questions come with collecting data about people? Collect only what you need and protect it, ask with consent and report honestly, keep the wording from pushing answers, and make the survey work for every group (design)

Status: Revision 3 (25 Nov 2026): preflight and fact repairs (see the final section, "Revision 3 (root, 25 November 2026)"). Revision 2 (24 Nov 2026): learning review resolved (see "Revision 2" below); not voiced. Revision 1 (24 Nov 2026): first design, written to the maths visual standard (`../maths-visual-standard.md`), `math-s11-d01.md` (Revision 1, this batch), the coherence audit and root's Standard rulings 1 to 99 (ruling 3: syllabus-only teaching where the site has no lesson). Not voiced. Next: student learning review and Codex maths check, then voicing on the Google voice and a build on the studio kit to grade A.

Narration 5,743 characters by script (see "Narration length estimate"; Revision 2), 13 scene headings, about 513 s with holds (key notes fixed at 45 s). Nothing recorded; human listening pending.

Scope: second video of the Year 11 Data analysis strand, outline playlist order 62. One video for Standard 1 and Standard 2. Viewers arrive from d01's final frame. Pre-design pack: `../pre-design/maths-standard/math-s11-d02.md`. Route entry: `math-s11-d02` in `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`. Site lessons: `year11/data-analysis/lesson02.sa.html` (card 06) and `lesson09.sa.html` (card 08, drill 2); privacy, ethics and diverse groups are taught from the syllabus (MSY-34). Visual system: maths studio kit; the bedroom, phone, exam desk, gym card and sports field plates (all existing); the records table, identifying filter, consent screen, lean gauge and audit checklist coded.

Owner rules applied: as d01 (header strip "DATA ANALYSIS" only; one question; one stage at a time; plain meanings; two attempts with "Pause here to answer." and 10 s countdowns; brief feedback with one crossed slip; five key notes with a framed card; everyday anchors; no people, hands or faces; cultural content kept general, owner rule of 18 November; Australian spelling; no em dashes).

Syllabus content point (Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11, Data analysis, "Statistical investigation process", common to Standard 1 and Standard 2), quoted from `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`:

- `ci63195120`: "Examine issues of privacy, bias, ethics and responsiveness to diverse groups and cultures"

Source: https://curriculum.nsw.edu.au/learning-areas/mathematics/mathematics-standard-11-12-2024/content/year-11/fa4de413b8

**Boundary:** starts from d01's final frame exactly (the bedroom `ms12-bedroom-furniture-v1.png`, about 1,000 px wide, at the left; the phone `ma12-phone-v1.png`, about 600 px tall, at the right with the fixed survey screen "How many hours did you sleep on your last school night?", buttons "under 7", "7 to under 8", "8 to under 9", "9 or more", and fields "Name: ______" and "Where does your phone charge overnight?"; chips "Who sees the answers?", "Next: privacy, bias and ethics" and "?"). Recalls d01 (the steps; the target population; the memory card) in grey chips. Teaches: privacy; ethics; bias from the asking; responsiveness to diverse groups and cultures. Not taught: sampling (d03); faults in experiments and observational studies (d04).

## Revision 2: learning review resolved (24 Nov 2026)

Source review: `../checks/m-s11-d02-learning-review.md`; resolution record `../checks/m-s11-d-learning-review-resolution.md`.

- **D02-FILTER (should fix, root's ruling 3): applied.** The third filter detail is now ordinary: "Add that one of them plays the cello. Now that one row, and its four hour answer, belongs to someone everyone can name." Chip "plays the cello", count 1; the dot's record row "Sleep (h): 4" slides out beside it, and the dot and row ring red on "name" (the bold cue moves from "is" to "name"). The counts 200, 24, 3, 1 stay. Author note (a) matches.
- **D02-MEDIAN (note): applied.** The group bar reads "24 in the band: typical sleep 7.5 h" (example label); "median" waits for d11.
- Length kept inside the strand range: "The first rule is simple. Only collect what you actually need." became "First, only collect what you actually need."; "And if you do need names" became "If you do need names"; scene 5's "Families also have different routines." was cut (the next sentence carries the point).
- Narration 5,755 characters (Revision 1: 5,766); about 514 s with holds, under the 570 s cap. Both attempts still end "Pause here to answer."; feedback about 24.6 s and 23.5 s. No em dash. Joins unchanged.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the name field.** d01's frame added "Name" and the phone question. The hook asks whether a student would admit to scrolling until 1 am with their name attached. That links the four ideas causally: privacy and fair wording are not only kind, they change the data.
- **Order: privacy, ethics, bias, diverse groups, then an audit.** The syllabus lists privacy, bias, ethics and responsiveness; the video moves ethics before bias so that consent and honest reporting sit beside privacy (both are about the people), and bias then leads into the diverse-groups scene (a survey that doesn't fit some groups also biases the results).
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Privacy ("people's right to control who sees information about them"); anonymous ("no one, not even the person running the survey, can tell whose answer is whose"); confidential ("the survey knows who you are, but keeps it to itself"); ethics ("treating the people who give you data fairly and honestly"); consent ("agreeing to take part, knowing what it's for"); bias ("a lean in the method that pushes results one way"); leading question ("a question that hints at the answer it wants").
- **Identifying by combination (simulation).** The 200-dot population narrows as details are added: in the band (24), a boarder (3), says 4 hours (1). "No name" is not the same as anonymous. Example counts.
- **Bias shown as a tilt (example data, labelled).** The same 20 sampled students: a leading question "Don't you agree phones in bedrooms ruin sleep?" gives 16 of 20 "agree"; the neutral question "Where does your phone charge overnight?" gives 12 bedroom and 8 elsewhere, and says nothing about ruin. The gauge tips, then levels. The 12 and 8 are the strand's sample (used again in d07, d14, d17).
- **Socially desirable answers.** People under-report things that sound bad when they can be identified; anonymity reduces this bias. One sentence links scenes 2 and 4.
- **Diverse groups, kept general (owner rule).** Not every student has their own bedroom or their own phone; some families have different evening routines, caring jobs or cultural and religious observances that change sleep times; some students read English as a second language or use a screen reader. Fixes: options that don't assume ("I share a room", "I don't have a phone", "prefer not to say"), translations and plain English, a paper copy, and trialling the survey with a few students from different groups before it goes out. No named community.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Identifying filter** (scene 2): the dot field narrows as detail chips are added, with a live count 200 → 24 → 3 → 1.
  2. **Lean gauge** (scene 4): a balance gauge over the 20 sample tokens; the leading wording tips it to "16 agree"; the neutral wording levels it and the tokens re-sort into "bedroom 12 | elsewhere 8".
  3. **Survey audit** (scene 6): a checklist sweeps the survey card; each failing item flashes, is fixed, and ticks green, with a counter "5 of 5".
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "need it?", "no name ≠ anonymous", "say what it's for", "skip any question", "report it all", "hints at an answer", "safe → honest", "fits every home?", "try it first". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The bedroom and phone (1); records table and filter (2); consent screen (3); lean gauge (4); inclusive survey card and paper copy (5); survey audit (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the population and the bus (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 2: "Name: ______" struck; row "keep the answer, drop the name" (framed green). Scene 4: "Don't you agree phones in bedrooms ruin sleep?" crossed; "Where does your phone charge overnight?" (framed green). Scene 6: the audited survey card (framed green).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Ask only what you need. Keep it safe. Ask it fairly. Make it fit everyone." Key line: "People answer honestly when they feel safe and the question doesn't push them."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): privacy and bias in a gym survey; crossed "it's fine, members agreed to join the gym" (caption "joining isn't consent to this survey"). A2 (pack question 2): online-only, English-only, "your son"; crossed "it's fair because anyone can open the link" (caption "not everyone can").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "No name means anonymous" (2); reporting only some results (3); leading wording (4, A1); one kind of household assumed (5, A2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a person who can be identified may hide the truth or be harmed, so collect only what you need and protect it, remembering that details can combine to identify someone (2); (2) people give data as a favour, so they must know what it's for, be free to say no, and be reported honestly (3); (3) wording that hints at an answer, or missing options, pushes results one way, and fear of being judged does the same, so the data lean (4); (4) a survey that doesn't fit some groups loses or distorts their answers, so the results no longer describe the whole target population (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (steps, question, target population, the memory card). Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** MSY-34 (privacy, ethics and diverse groups have no site teaching). The site's nightclub example is not used.
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d03, sampling methods).** Scene 12: board clear; the 200-dot population field (`DotField`, about 1,000 px wide) at the centre: 140 dots blue and 60 dots blue with an amber outline, legend chips "140 live nearby" and "60 catch the early bus"; the bus `ma12-bus-side-v1.png` (about 420 px wide) at the bottom right; chips "Who do we ask?", "Next: sampling methods" and "?". d03 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) Filter counts 200, 24, 3, 1 are examples (in the band; a boarder; plays the cello). The 4 h answer is the exposed answer, not a filter (Revision 2).
  (b) Lean gauge: 16 of 20 is an example of a leading-question result, labelled "example". The neutral counts 12 and 8 are the strand's sample (bedroom 12; elsewhere 8: kitchen 5, lounge room 2, other 1 in d07).
  (c) The population split 140 and 60 is d03's strata (70% and 30%).

Main question: *Would you admit to scrolling until 1 am if your name were on the answer? What privacy, bias and ethics questions come with collecting data about people?*
Entry knowledge (math-s11-d01): the investigation steps; statistical questions; target population; the survey card.
Stops after: privacy, ethics, bias from the asking, diverse groups, an audit.
Handoff: math-s11-d03: "Next: sampling methods".

teaching.task: # Maths S11 D02: What privacy, bias and ethics questions come with collecting data about people? Collect only what you need and protect it, ask with consent and report honestly, keep the wording from pushing answers, and make the survey work for every group (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Start with privacy, people's right to control who sees information about them. First, only collect what you actually need. Our question is about sleep, so we don't need anyone's name. Drop it, and the survey becomes anonymous, meaning no one, not even the person running it, can tell whose answer is whose. But be careful. Leaving out names isn't always enough. Say the survey also asks if you're in the band, and if you board at the school. In the band leaves twenty-four students. A boarder in the band, just three. Add that one of them plays the cello. Now that one row, and its four hour answer, belongs to someone everyone can name. So report results for groups, never for one person. If you do need names, say to follow someone up, keep them separate and private. That's called confidential. Next, ethics, which means treating the people who give you data fairly and honestly. People are doing you a favour, so they need consent, agreeing to take part, knowing what it's for. Tell them what the survey is for, who will see the answers, and that taking part is their choice. They can skip any question, or stop. At school, students under eighteen also need the school's permission, and often a parent's. Don't ask anything that could embarrass or hurt someone for no good reason. And when the results come in, report all of them, including the ones you didn't expect. Reporting only the answers that suit your story is just as unfair as asking an unfair question. Bias is a lean in the method that pushes results one way. Some of it comes from who you ask, and that's coming up. But a lot comes from how you ask. Here's a leading question, one that hints at the answer it wants. Don't you agree that phones in bedrooms ruin sleep? Ask our twenty students that, and sixteen might agree, just to be agreeable. Now ask it neutrally. Where does your phone charge overnight? Twelve say their bedroom, and eight say somewhere else. That's data we can actually use. Missing options lean results too. If the only choices are bedroom and kitchen, where does everyone else go? And remember the name field. People who feel judged give the answer that sounds good. So privacy isn't just polite. Feeling safe is what makes people honest.

teaching.openingDecision: Visual: opens on d01's final frame exactly. On "Our survey now asks" the "Next" chips fade; "Name: ______" and the phone question pulse violet. On "scrolling in bed" a small coded phone-glow sits on the bedroom plate's pillow with a clock chip "1:00 am". teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn. A gym's survey asks for your full name and mobile number. It also asks, don't you agree our new opening hours are better? Identify one privacy problem and one bias problem, and fix each one. Pause here to answer. Last one. A council's survey about a new sports field is online only, it's only in English, and it asks, which sport does your son play? Give two ways it fails to respond to diverse groups, and a fix for each. Pause here to answer.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the name field.** d01's frame added "Name" and the phone question. The hook asks whether a student would admit to scrolling until 1 am with their name attached. That links the four ideas causally: privacy and fair wording are not only kind, they change the data.
- **Order: privacy, ethics, bias, diverse groups, then an audit.** The syllabus lists privacy, bias, ethics and responsiveness; the video moves ethics before bias so that consent and honest reporting sit beside privacy (both are about the people), and bias then leads into the diverse-groups scene (a survey that doesn't fit some groups also biases the results).
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Privacy ("people's right to control who sees information about them"); anonymous ("no one, not even the person running the survey, can tell whose answer is whose"); confidential ("the survey knows who you are, but keeps it to itself"); ethics ("treating the people who give you data fairly and honestly"); consent ("agreeing to take part, knowing what it's for"); bias ("a lean in the method that pushes results one way"); leading question ("a question that hints at the answer it wants").
- **Identifying by combination (simulation).** The 200-dot population narrows as details are added: in the band (24), a boarder (3), says 4 hours (1). "No name" is not the same as anonymous. Example counts.
- **Bias shown as a tilt (example data, labelled).** The same 20 sampled students: a leading question "Don't you agree phones in bedrooms ruin sleep?" gives 16 of 20 "agree"; the neutral question "Where does your phone charge overnight?" gives 12 bedroom and 8 elsewhere, and says nothing about ruin. The gauge tips, then levels. The 12 and 8 are the strand's sample (used again in d07, d14, d17).
- **Socially desirable answers.** People under-report things that sound bad when they can be identified; anonymity reduces this bias. One sentence links scenes 2 and 4.
- **Diverse groups, kept general (owner rule).** Not every student has their own bedroom or their own phone; some families have different evening routines, caring jobs or cultural and religious observances that change sleep times; some students read English as a second language or use a screen reader. Fixes: options that don't assume ("I share a room", "I don't have a phone", "prefer not to say"), translations and plain English, a paper copy, and trialling the survey with a few students from different groups before it goes out. No named community.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Identifying filter** (scene 2): the dot field narrows as detail chips are added, with a live count 200 → 24 → 3 → 1.
  2. **Lean gauge** (scene 4): a balance gauge over the 20 sample tokens; the leading wording tips it to "16 agree"; the neutral wording levels it and the tokens re-sort into "bedroom 12 | elsewhere 8".
  3. **Survey audit** (scene 6): a checklist sweeps the survey card; each failing item flashes, is fixed, and ticks green, with a counter "5 of 5".
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "need it?", "no name ≠ anonymous", "say what it's for", "skip any question", "report it all", "hints at an answer", "safe → honest", "fits every home?", "try it first". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The bedroom and phone (1); records table and filter (2); consent screen (3); lean gauge (4); inclusive survey card and paper copy (5); survey audit (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the population and the bus (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 2: "Name: ______" struck; row "keep the answer, drop the name" (framed green). Scene 4: "Don't you agree phones in bedrooms ruin sleep?" crossed; "Where does your phone charge overnight?" (framed green). Scene 6: the audited survey card (framed green).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Ask only what you need. Keep it safe. Ask it fairly. Make it fit everyone." Key line: "People answer honestly when they feel safe and the question doesn't push them."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): privacy and bias in a gym survey; crossed "it's fine, members agreed to join the gym" (caption "joining isn't consent to this survey"). A2 (pack question 2): online-only, English-only, "your son"; crossed "it's fair because anyone can open the link" (caption "not everyone can").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "No name means anonymous" (2); reporting only some results (3); leading wording (4, A1); one kind of household assumed (5, A2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a person who can be identified may hide the truth or be harmed, so collect only what you need and protect it, remembering that details can combine to identify someone (2); (2) people give data as a favour, so they must know what it's for, be free to say no, and be reported honestly (3); (3) wording that hints at an answer, or missing options, pushes results one way, and fear of being judged does the same, so the data lean (4); (4) a survey that doesn't fit some groups loses or distorts their answers, so the results no longer describe the whole target population (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (steps, question, target population, the memory card). Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** MSY-34 (privacy, ethics and diverse groups have no site teaching). The site's nightclub example is not used.
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d03, sampling methods).** Scene 12: board clear; the 200-dot population field (`DotField`, about 1,000 px wide) at the centre: 140 dots blue and 60 dots blue with an amber outline, legend chips "140 live nearby" and "60 catch the early bus"; the bus `ma12-bus-side-v1.png` (about 420 px wide) at the bottom right; chips "Who do we ask?", "Next: sampling methods" and "?". d03 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) Filter counts 200, 24, 3, 1 are examples (in the band; a boarder; plays the cello). The 4 h answer is the exposed answer, not a filter (Revision 2).
  (b) Lean gauge: 16 of 20 is an example of a leading-question result, labelled "example". The neutral counts 12 and 8 are the strand's sample (bedroom 12; elsewhere 8: kitchen 5, lounge room 2, other 1 in d07).
  (c) The population split 140 and 60 is d03's strata (70% and 30%).

scenes.teachingReason: Start with privacy, people's right to control who sees information about them. First, only collect what you actually need. Our question is about sleep, so we don't need anyone's name. Drop it, and the survey becomes anonymous, meaning no one, not even the person running it, can tell whose answer is whose. But be careful. If you do need names, say to follow someone up, keep them separate and private. That's called confidential.

scenes.teachingReason: Next, ethics, which means treating the people who give you data fairly and honestly. People are doing you a favour, so they need consent, agreeing to take part, knowing what it's for. Tell them what the survey is for, who will see the answers, and that taking part is their choice. They can skip any question, or stop. At school, students under eighteen also need the school's permission, and often a parent's. Don't ask anything that could embarrass or hurt someone for no good reason. And when the results come in, report all of them, including the ones you didn't expect. Reporting only the answers that suit your story is just as unfair as asking an unfair question.

scenes.teachingReason: Bias is a lean in the method that pushes results one way. Some of it comes from who you ask, and that's coming up. But a lot comes from how you ask. Here's a leading question, one that hints at the answer it wants. Don't you agree that phones in bedrooms ruin sleep? Ask our twenty students that, and sixteen might agree, just to be agreeable. Now ask it neutrally. Where does your phone charge overnight? Twelve say their bedroom, and eight say somewhere else. That's data we can actually use. Missing options lean results too. If the only choices are bedroom and kitchen, where does everyone else go? And remember the name field. People who feel judged give the answer that sounds good. So privacy isn't just polite. Feeling safe is what makes people honest.

scenes.teachingReason: A survey also has to work for everyone in the target population, not just students like the person who wrote it. Our phone question assumes every student has their own phone and their own bedroom. Some share a room, and some don't have a phone. So add options like I share a room, I don't have a phone, and prefer not to say. Some students care for younger siblings, work late shifts, or keep cultural or religious practices that change when they sleep. The survey shouldn't treat any of that as wrong. Some students read English as a second language, or use a screen reader. Plain English, a translation, or a paper copy lets them answer too. And before it goes out, try the survey with a few students from different groups, and fix whatever confuses them. Leave a group out, and the results describe fewer people than you claimed.

scenes.teachingReason: Let's audit the whole survey. Do we need every question? The name's gone. Is it anonymous, or at least confidential, and reported in groups? Yes. Does everyone know what it's for, and that they can skip or stop? Yes. Is every question neutral, with an option for every answer? Yes. Does it work for every group in the target population? With the new options, the translation and the paper copy, it does. Five ticks. Now the answers we collect have a fair chance of being true, and of describing the people we said they would.

scenes.teachingReason: Privacy first. The survey doesn't need your name and number, and they link your answers to you, so drop them, or keep them separate and confidential. Bias next. Don't you agree leads you to say yes. Ask how well the new hours suit you, with balanced choices. Saying it's fine because members agreed to join the gym is the slip.

scenes.teachingReason: Our survey is clear, fair and safe. Now, who gets it? There are two hundred Year 11 students at our school. A hundred and forty live nearby, and sixty catch the early bus, so they get up sooner. We can't easily ask all two hundred, so we'll ask twenty. But which twenty? Pick the wrong way, and the sample won't look like the population. That's next.
